sram-flash-001.question: Which correctly describes the structure of a typical six-transistor SRAM cell?
choices: Two cross-coupled inverters and two access transistors
Six floating-gate transistors connected in series
sram-flash-001.explanation: A 6T SRAM cell combines a latch of two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors), each feeding the other's input, with two access transistors connecting it to the bit lines. Positive feedback holds its state, so no refresh is needed while powered. At about 120–150F² it is roughly 20 times larger than a DRAM cell, but it is built in the same process as logic and is fast, making it the workhorse of CPU caches.

sram-flash-002.question: Compared with NOR flash, which is a characteristic of NAND flash memory?
choices: Fast random access, suitable for executing program code directly
Cells are connected in series, so it is easy to make dense and suits high-capacity storage
It is volatile memory that loses data when the power is off
sram-flash-002.explanation: NAND flash strings dozens of cells in series and omits per-cell contacts, so area per bit is small and it suits high-capacity SSDs and memory cards. Reading through the series string is slower, though, so access is page-based. NOR flash connects each cell in parallel to the bit line, giving fast random reads suited to executing code in place. Both are non-volatile.

sram-flash-003.question: In flash memory, what is the scheme that stores 3 bits of information in one memory cell called?
sram-flash-003.explanation: By bits per cell, flash is SLC (1 bit), MLC (2), TLC (3) or QLC (4). TLC distinguishes eight threshold-voltage states and stores three times as much as SLC in the same cells. More bits lower cost but narrow the gaps between states, hurting endurance, speed and retention. TLC dominates mainstream SSDs today, with QLC growing for high-capacity drives.

sram-flash-004.question: Which correctly describes how data is written to and erased from flash memory?
choices: Charge is stored in a capacitor
The magnetization direction of a magnetic layer is changed
Electrons are moved into or out of a floating gate or charge-trap layer, changing the transistor's threshold voltage
sram-flash-004.explanation: A flash cell is a transistor with a floating gate (or charge-trap layer) beneath its control gate that stores electrons. Moving electrons in or out with high voltage—by tunneling, for example—shifts the threshold voltage, which distinguishes 0 from 1. Surrounded by insulating films a few nm thick, the electrons are retained for about ten years without power. Reading applies a set gate voltage and checks whether current flows.

sram-flash-005.question: Which correctly describes 3D NAND flash memory?
choices: Memory cells are stacked vertically in many layers to increase capacity
It operates on three different supply voltages
sram-flash-005.explanation: As planar scaling neared its limit around 15 nm, 3D NAND, which stacks cells vertically, entered mass production around 2013 and became mainstream. Deep cylindrical channel holes are etched through a thick stack of alternating conductive and insulating layers, and cells are formed on the hole walls. Capacity grows without shrinking cells aggressively, and interference drops. Three bits per cell is TLC, commonly combined with 3D NAND.

sram-flash-006.question: What is the main reason flash memory has a limited number of rewrite cycles?
choices: Repeated rewriting degrades the tunnel oxide that electrons pass through
sram-flash-006.explanation: Each program or erase drives electrons through the tunnel oxide at fields around 10 MV/cm, and some become trapped or create defects. Repeated cycling narrows the threshold-voltage window and makes stored electrons leak more easily (stress-induced leakage current, SILC). Endurance is therefore limited, and multilevel cells with narrow state gaps suffer most: about 100,000 cycles for SLC versus a few thousand for TLC.

sram-flash-007.question: What is the purpose of wear leveling, used in SSDs and similar devices?
choices: To compress data and increase capacity
To spread writes across the whole device instead of concentrating them on certain blocks, extending its life
sram-flash-007.explanation: Each block tolerates a limited number of erase cycles, so writing the same logical address repeatedly would wear one spot out early. With wear leveling, the controller maintains a logical-to-physical mapping (the FTL) and steers writes to blocks with fewer erases. It also occasionally relocates rarely changed static data, evening out wear across all blocks and extending product life.

sram-flash-008.question: What is the unit in which data is erased in NAND flash memory?
sram-flash-008.explanation: NAND reads and programs by page (around 16 KB), but erases only by block—hundreds to thousands of pages, several to tens of MB—because erase applies high voltage to an entire well to remove electrons in bulk. Even partial updates cannot overwrite in place: new data goes to a free page, the old page is marked invalid, and garbage collection later erases blocks in bulk.

sram-flash-009.question: Which correctly describes a property of SRAM?
choices: It retains data without refresh while powered, but loses data when the power is turned off
It retains data when the power is turned off
sram-flash-009.explanation: SRAM holds data through the positive feedback of a latch, so it needs no refresh while powered, but it is volatile and loses data when power is removed. Access takes around 1 ns, making it the choice for CPU caches and register files. Transistor leakage flows even in standby, so large arrays face standby-power problems and use low-voltage retention modes.

sram-flash-010.question: In charge-trap cells, widely used in 3D NAND, which material is commonly used for the layer that stores charge?
sram-flash-010.explanation: A charge-trap cell stores electrons in trap states within an insulating silicon nitride film instead of a conductive floating gate. Because the charge stays localized, a single defect in the dielectric cannot drain all of it, and interference with neighboring cells is small. The SiO2/SiN/SiO2 (ONO) stack can be deposited continuously on channel-hole walls, making it well suited to vertically stacked 3D NAND.

sram-flash-011.question: Under which condition does the data retention of flash memory tend to degrade?
choices: When stored in a dark place
sram-flash-011.explanation: Stored electrons gain thermal energy and escape through the dielectric more easily at high temperature, so retention shortens when stored hot. This is exploited in accelerated tests that bake devices to estimate long-term retention quickly (the Arrhenius model). Oxide worn by many program/erase cycles worsens retention further, so leaving a heavily used SSD unpowered for long periods is best avoided.

sram-flash-012.question: In recent advanced processes, what is the most appropriate reason SRAM cell area has become harder to shrink than logic?
choices: SRAM is sensitive to variations in transistor characteristics, making it hard to secure margins for stable reading and writing
sram-flash-012.explanation: An SRAM cell's stability depends on balancing the drive strengths of six near-minimum-size transistors. With scaling, variation from effects such as random dopant fluctuation grows relative to device size, making it hard to keep read and write margins even for the worst of hundreds of millions of cells. In recent nodes SRAM cell area has shrunk much less than logic, so cache area has become a growing share of the die.

sram-flash-013.question: Which technique do NAND flash controllers use to cope with the increase in read errors that comes with storing more bits per cell?
choices: Powerful error-correcting codes (such as LDPC codes)
sram-flash-013.explanation: The more bits stored per cell, the narrower the gaps between threshold-voltage distributions and the more read errors occur. NAND controllers therefore use powerful error correction such as LDPC codes, adding hundreds of bytes of parity per few KB of data. LDPC can use soft-decision information about how likely each bit is, so controllers re-read at shifted read voltages to boost correction capability further.

sram-flash-014.question: What is a typical use of NOR flash memory?
choices: Storing program code for devices (such as boot programs)
sram-flash-014.explanation: NOR flash connects each cell in parallel to the bit line for fast random access, so a CPU can fetch and run code directly from it (execute in place, XIP). It is used for boot code, microcontroller firmware and automotive control software. Capacities are small (a few Mbit to a few Gbit) and cost per bit is higher than NAND, so bulk data storage uses NAND.

sram-flash-015.question: Which correctly describes garbage collection in an SSD?
choices: Moving valid data out of blocks that contain invalid data, then erasing those blocks to create free space
sram-flash-015.explanation: NAND cannot overwrite in place and erases only by block, so each rewrite leaves the old version behind as an invalid page. The controller picks blocks with many invalid pages, moves their valid data to another block, and erases them to create free space. These extra copies cause write amplification, and the fuller the drive, the more often garbage collection runs and the more write performance suffers.

sram-flash-016.question: In an SRAM read, what is the operation called that charges the bit lines in advance to the supply voltage or similar?
sram-flash-016.explanation: To read SRAM, the bit-line pair is first precharged to the supply voltage; when the word line selects a cell, the bit line on the side storing 0 discharges slightly through the access transistor. The sense amplifier fires once a difference of tens to about a hundred mV develops, without waiting for a full swing, which makes reads fast. The bit lines are then precharged again for the next access.

sram-flash-017.question: Which electron injection mechanism is mainly used for writing (programming) NAND flash memory?
choices: Movement of electrons by a magnetic field
sram-flash-017.explanation: NAND programs by applying around 20 V to the control gate so electrons tunnel from the channel through the thin tunnel oxide into the storage layer—Fowler-Nordheim (FN) tunneling. The current per cell is tiny, so the more than one hundred thousand cells in a page can be programmed at once. NOR flash often uses channel hot-electron injection, accelerating electrons with drain voltage, which is faster but draws more current.

sram-flash-018.question: In NAND flash, what is the phenomenon in which repeatedly reading the same block gradually shifts the threshold voltages of cells that are not being read?
sram-flash-018.explanation: Reading NAND applies a pass voltage of several volts to unselected cells so they conduct, and repeated reads slowly inject electrons that raise their threshold voltages—read disturb, which becomes significant after tens to hundreds of thousands of reads. It affects blocks holding frequently read data, so controllers count reads and rewrite the data to another block as the limit approaches.

sram-flash-019.question: In QLC (4 bits per cell) NAND flash, how many threshold voltage states must one cell distinguish?
sram-flash-019.explanation: Storing N bits per cell requires distinguishing 2ᴺ threshold-voltage states—2⁴ = 16 for QLC. The usable voltage window (a few volts) is about the same, so the spacing between states is a small fraction of SLC's, demanding much finer programming control. QLC therefore writes slowly and endures less but is cheaper per gigabyte, used in read-heavy data-center and high-capacity SSDs.

sram-flash-020.question: In TLC and QLC SSDs, what is the main purpose of using part of the space as SLC to absorb writes temporarily?
sram-flash-020.explanation: TLC and QLC take time to program because states must be placed precisely. SSDs therefore run part of their free space in SLC mode, writing there quickly first and migrating data to TLC/QLC areas when idle (an SLC cache). If sustained writes overflow the cache, speed drops sharply to the native rate, which is why large file copies can slow down midway.

sram-flash-021.question: What problem tends to occur as the supply voltage of SRAM is lowered?
choices: The margin for stable reading and writing (noise margin) shrinks, making malfunctions more likely
sram-flash-021.explanation: An SRAM cell works by balancing latch stability against access-transistor drive. Lowering the supply voltage shrinks noise margins and magnifies transistor variation, making read upsets and write failures more likely. As a result, SRAM's minimum operating voltage (Vmin) often sets the floor for the whole chip's supply, a barrier to voltage scaling.

sram-flash-022.question: What is the advantage of an 8T SRAM cell, which adds read-only transistors to a 6T SRAM cell?
choices: The cell area is smaller than 6T
Data remains when power is turned off
Cell data is less likely to be disturbed during reads, so it operates stably even at low voltage
sram-flash-022.explanation: In a 6T cell, bit-line charge can push up the storage node during a read and flip the data. An 8T cell adds a two-transistor read-only path; the storage node only drives a gate there, so reads cannot disturb it. Read and write transistors can be optimized separately, improving low-voltage stability, and separate read and write ports can operate simultaneously. The cost is a larger cell.

sram-flash-023.question: In flash memory erase, what happens to a cell's threshold voltage when electrons are removed from the floating gate or similar layer?
sram-flash-023.explanation: Electrons (negative charge) on the floating gate cancel part of the gate voltage, so more voltage is needed to form a channel and the threshold rises. Erasing removes electrons and lowers the threshold; programming adds them and raises it. NAND conventionally treats the erased (low-threshold) state as "1" and the programmed state as "0," which is why erased flash reads as 0xFF.

sram-flash-024.question: Which is closest to the number of layers in recent 3D NAND?
sram-flash-024.explanation: 3D NAND started at 24 layers around 2013 and has added layers every generation; products above 200 layers are in mass production and 300+ layers have appeared. Taller stacks make it harder to etch holes several µm deep with uniform diameter top to bottom, so the stack is built in two or more decks whose holes are joined (string stacking). Thinner layers are also used to limit total height.

sram-flash-025.question: In NAND flash, what is the role of the select transistors placed at both ends of the series-connected memory cells?
choices: To connect or disconnect the string (series of cells) being read or written to the bit line and source line
sram-flash-025.explanation: Each NAND string of dozens to hundreds of series cells has select transistors at both ends, on the bit-line (drain) side and the source-line side, connecting only the string being accessed. During programming, unselected strings are cut off so their channels float and are boosted by capacitive coupling to the gates (self-boosting), preventing unintended programming.

sram-flash-026.question: When writing to an SRAM cell, one bit line is pulled down to 0 V to flip the cell's state. What condition is required of the access transistor?
choices: It must have sufficiently stronger drive than the pull-up transistor (pMOS) in the cell
It must be weaker than every transistor in the cell
sram-flash-026.explanation: To write, the access transistor must pull the storage node to 0, overpowering the pull-up pMOS trying to hold 1, so the access transistor is made substantially stronger than the pMOS (the pull-up ratio). For read stability it must also be weaker than the pull-down nMOS (the cell ratio). Balancing these three drive strengths is the heart of SRAM cell design.

sram-flash-027.question: In NAND flash, which programming method applies repeated program pulses with gradually increasing voltage, checking the threshold voltage after each one?
sram-flash-027.explanation: ISPP applies program pulses starting around 15 V, for example, and raises the voltage by a few hundred mV each step, verifying the threshold voltage after every pulse. Cells that reach their target are inhibited by raising their bit-line voltage, so even cells that vary end up in a tight threshold distribution. Smaller steps tighten the distribution but take longer, trading speed against multilevel precision.

sram-flash-028.question: Which command notifies an SSD of space freed by files deleted by the OS, making garbage collection more efficient?
sram-flash-028.explanation: Deleting a file only updates the OS's bookkeeping, so the SSD does not know the data is obsolete and keeps copying it during garbage collection. The TRIM command tells the SSD which ranges are no longer needed; it marks those pages invalid and can erase them without copying, reducing write amplification and improving performance and lifespan. NVMe provides the same function through the Deallocate command.

sram-flash-029.question: Which non-volatile memory has been integrated on the same chip as logic circuits to store microcontroller programs?
sram-flash-029.explanation: Microcontrollers have long integrated embedded flash on the same die as logic to store programs and data. It keeps its contents without power and allows firmware updates after shipment. But it adds many process steps, such as forming floating gates, and is hard to integrate beyond about 28 nm or with high-k/metal gates, so MRAM and ReRAM, which need fewer extra steps, are replacing it.

sram-flash-030.question: Which orders SLC, MLC and TLC from the most rewrite cycles to the fewest?
sram-flash-030.explanation: Fewer bits per cell mean wider gaps between threshold states, so cells still read correctly as wear broadens the distributions, giving higher endurance. Generally SLC > MLC > TLC > QLC, roughly 100,000 cycles for SLC, several thousand to 10,000 for MLC, a few thousand for TLC and about 1,000 for QLC. SLC mode is used in industrial products needing high endurance and in SSD cache areas.

sram-flash-031.question: Which correctly describes flash memory?
choices: It is non-volatile memory that retains data after power is removed
It is volatile memory that loses data when power is removed
sram-flash-031.explanation: Flash memory traps electrons in floating gates or charge-trap layers surrounded by insulators, so it retains data without power—it is non-volatile. Retention is typically about ten years, shortened by heat and program/erase wear. It was invented in the 1980s by Fujio Masuoka at Toshiba and named for erasing in one go, like a camera flash.
choiceNotes: Correct. Flash memory is non-volatile.
DRAM and SRAM are the memories that lose data at power-off.
DRAM is the memory that needs periodic refresh.

sram-flash-032.question: Which memory is mainly used in USB flash drives and SD cards?
sram-flash-032.explanation: USB drives, SD cards and SSDs use NAND flash, an inexpensive high-capacity non-volatile memory, together with a controller that handles error correction and wear leveling. Cheap products may have simple controllers and weaker long-term reliability. DRAM and SRAM are volatile and lose data without power, so they are not used for portable storage.
choiceNotes: SRAM is volatile and mainly used for caches and similar.
Correct. High-capacity, non-volatile NAND flash is used.
DRAM is volatile and mainly used as main memory.

sram-flash-033.question: How many bits does an SLC (single-level cell) flash memory store per cell?
sram-flash-033.explanation: SLC stores one bit (two states) per cell. Because states are easy to distinguish, it programs fast, endures about 100,000 cycles and handles retention and heat well, but offers the least capacity for a given number of cells. It is therefore used in industrial and automotive applications demanding high reliability. MLC stores 2 bits, TLC 3 and QLC 4.
choiceNotes: Two bits per cell is MLC.
Four bits per cell is QLC.
Correct. SLC stores one bit per cell.

sram-flash-034.question: Which correctly describes an SSD compared with an HDD (hard disk drive)?
choices: It records magnetically on spinning disks
It has no mechanically moving parts, offering fast random access and shock resistance
It is always cheaper than an HDD for the same capacity
sram-flash-034.explanation: An SSD records data in NAND flash and has no moving parts such as platters or heads. An HDD needs several ms per access for head movement and rotational delay, whereas an SSD takes tens to about 100 µs, making random access hundreds of times faster. SSDs are also shock-resistant and silent. HDDs remain cheaper per terabyte and are still used for bulk storage.
choiceNotes: Recording magnetically on spinning disks is how an HDD works.
Correct. It has no moving parts, making it fast and shock-resistant.
Price per capacity generally tends to be lower for HDDs.

sram-flash-035.question: What is the most appropriate main use of SRAM?
choices: Long-term storage of large amounts of data
sram-flash-035.explanation: SRAM needs no refresh, is built in the same process as logic and can be accessed in about 1 ns, so it is used for CPU caches (L1–L3) and register files. Some recent CPUs carry tens to hundreds of MB of L3 cache, and products that stack extra SRAM dies vertically have appeared. Its large area per bit and high cost make it unsuitable for bulk main memory.
choiceNotes: Recording media use non-volatile NAND flash.
SRAM is volatile and cannot be used for long-term storage.
Correct. Fast SRAM is used for caches.

sram-flash-036.question: In NAND flash memory, what is needed to write new data to a page that already contains data?
choices: Erase the block containing the page first, then write
Overwrite it with a lower write voltage
sram-flash-036.explanation: Programming NAND can only raise threshold voltages (1→0); returning requires an erase, and erases happen only in blocks larger than a page, so in-place overwriting is impossible. The SSD controller writes new data to a free page, updates the logical-to-physical map (FTL) to invalidate the old page, and erases blocks in bulk later. This mechanism underlies SSD performance and lifetime management.
choiceNotes: Correct. Data can only be written after erasing.
NAND flash cannot be overwritten.
Lowering the voltage does not make overwriting possible.

sram-flash-037.question: Which correctly describes the difference between EEPROM and flash memory?
choices: EEPROM is volatile and flash memory is non-volatile
EEPROM can be rewritten byte by byte, while flash memory erases in larger units such as blocks
sram-flash-037.explanation: EEPROM is non-volatile memory that can be erased and rewritten byte by byte; each cell needs its own select transistor, so cells are large and capacities range from a few Kbit to a few Mbit. It endures about a million write cycles, suiting device settings and calibration data. Flash erases in whole blocks, eliminating per-cell select transistors to shrink the cell and reach high capacity.
choiceNotes: EEPROM is electrically erasable and rewritable ROM.
Both EEPROM and flash memory are non-volatile.
Correct. They differ in rewrite granularity.

sram-flash-038.question: Which correctly describes the static noise margin (SNM) that represents the stability of an SRAM cell?
choices: The amount of noise voltage the cell can withstand without flipping its stored state, obtained from the butterfly curve
The current consumption of the cell
The time taken to read the cell
sram-flash-038.explanation: SNM is the side of the largest square that fits inside the butterfly curve formed by overlaying the transfer characteristics of a cell's two inverters; larger means more noise-tolerant. Read SNM, with the access transistor on, is smaller than hold SNM and is the binding stability constraint. It shrinks with lower supply voltage or greater variation, making it a key metric in low-voltage design.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is the noise margin obtained from the butterfly curve.
Current consumption is a separate characteristic from SNM.
Read time is the access time, not the SNM.

sram-flash-039.question: Which is closest to the typical endurance (number of rewrite cycles) of SLC NAND flash memory?
sram-flash-039.explanation: SLC endurance is about 50,000–100,000 cycles, falling with more bits per cell: several thousand to 10,000 for MLC, a few thousand for TLC and about 1,000 for QLC. The main limit is gradual tunnel-oxide degradation with each cycle. SSD endurance is rated in TBW (total bytes written) or DWPD (drive writes per day) and is extended through wear leveling and spare area.
choiceNotes: About 100 is far too few for SLC.
Correct. SLC is typically about 100,000 cycles.
About 100 million is far too many for flash memory.

sram-flash-040.question: Which correctly describes "bad block management" in NAND flash?
choices: Bad blocks found at manufacturing or during use are recorded, excluded from use and replaced with spare blocks
Chips with even one bad block are not shipped
Bad blocks are repaired with a high voltage
sram-flash-040.explanation: NAND ships with the expectation of some bad blocks (up to a few percent), and wear creates more during use. The controller reads factory bad-block markers into a table, adds blocks that fail erase or program in the field, retires them and substitutes spares. This management lets imperfect chips operate correctly as a whole.
choiceNotes: Correct. Bad blocks are avoided and replaced with spares.
NAND flash is shipped on the assumption that it contains some bad blocks.
Worn-out blocks cannot be repaired with a voltage.

sram-flash-041.question: Which correctly describes "overprovisioning" in an SSD?
choices: Writing data in two places for redundancy
Installing more flash memory than the capacity shown to the user and using the extra area for garbage collection and longer life
Installing less flash memory than the displayed capacity
sram-flash-041.explanation: Over-provisioning installs more flash than the user-visible capacity and uses the surplus for free blocks, garbage collection and bad-block replacement. Fitting 512 GiB of NAND into a drive sold as 480 GB, for example, leaves about 14% spare. More spare area eases garbage collection, stabilizing write performance and extending life, so enterprise SSDs reserve more.
choiceNotes: Duplicating data is mirroring, a different mechanism.
Correct. The extra area is used for internal management.
With less than the displayed capacity, the stated capacity could not be used.

sram-flash-042.question: Which correctly describes "write amplification" in an SSD?
choices: The write voltage becoming higher than normal
The amount of data actually written to flash exceeding the amount written by the host
sram-flash-042.explanation: Because flash cannot overwrite and erases by block, garbage collection adds extra writes such as copying valid data to new blocks, so the flash receives more data than the host wrote. The ratio is the write amplification factor (WAF), which can reach several times under small random writes. TRIM, spare area and data compression reduce it, protecting lifespan and performance.
choiceNotes: Write amplification degrades rather than improves performance.
It has nothing to do with voltage.
Correct. More data is actually written than the host wrote.

sram-flash-043.question: What is the basic unit for reading and writing (programming) in NAND flash memory?
sram-flash-043.explanation: NAND reads and programs by page (several to over ten KB, about 16 KB in recent devices) and erases by block (hundreds to thousands of pages). A page corresponds to the cells on one word line, and multilevel cells map several pages to each word line (three for TLC). The mismatch between program and erase units is the fundamental reason management such as garbage collection is needed.
choiceNotes: The block is the unit of erasure.
Correct. Reading and writing are done per page.
Reads and writes are not done on the whole chip at once.

sram-flash-044.question: Which interface standard, built on PCI Express, is widely used to connect high-speed SSDs to the host?
sram-flash-044.explanation: NVMe (NVM Express) is designed to drive flash efficiently over PCI Express and supports up to 64K command queues in parallel. Compared with SATA (AHCI: one queue of up to 32 commands, about 600 MB/s maximum) built for HDDs, it offers lower latency and higher bandwidth—about 7 GB/s with PCIe 4.0 x4 and over 10 GB/s with PCIe 5.0. It is widely used in compact M.2 SSDs.
choiceNotes: IDE is an old parallel interface for HDDs.
USB 1.1 is a slow general-purpose interface.
Correct. It is the standard for high-speed PCIe SSDs.

sram-flash-045.question: In SRAM, which correctly describes the "data retention voltage" that sets the lower limit when the supply is lowered during standby to reduce leakage?
choices: The lowest supply voltage at which the cell keeps its contents without being read or written
The maximum voltage needed for reading
sram-flash-045.explanation: In standby, with no reads or writes, an SRAM cell can retain data at voltages below its operating supply. The lowest voltage that preserves data is the data retention voltage (DRV), typically a few hundred mV. Lowering the supply to just above it in standby cuts leakage sharply, reducing standby power several-fold. Smartphone SoCs use this to keep cache contents during sleep.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is the lowest supply voltage that preserves the contents.
The data retention voltage concerns the lowest voltage.
Writing requires a higher voltage than retention.

sram-flash-046.question: In a 6T SRAM cell, which design is needed so that the cell contents are not flipped during a read (to prevent read upset)?
choices: Make the access transistor stronger than the pull-down transistor
Make the pull-down (driver) transistor stronger than the access transistor
sram-flash-046.explanation: During a read, current flows from the precharged bit line through the access transistor into the node holding 0, raising its voltage slightly. If the pull-down transistor is sufficiently stronger than the access transistor (a cell ratio β = pull-down/access of about 1.5–2.5), the rise stays below the opposite inverter's switching threshold and the data does not flip. 8T cells and read-assist circuits also address this.
choiceNotes: A too-strong access transistor makes the cell more likely to flip during reads.
Without pull-up transistors, the cell cannot hold a 1.
Correct. A stronger pull-down limits the rise at the node holding 0.

sram-flash-047.question: Which is an example of a "write assist" technique to prevent SRAM write failures at low voltage?
choices: Pulling the bit line on the 0 side slightly below ground during a write
Raising the cell supply voltage during a write
sram-flash-047.explanation: At low voltage, the access transistor may lack the drive to overpower the cell's pull-up, causing write failures. The negative bit-line technique pulls the bit line on the 0 side below ground (about −100 to −200 mV), increasing the access transistor's gate-source voltage and easing the write. Lowering the cell supply during writes to weaken the pull-up is also used; such assist circuits are essential in advanced-node SRAM.
choiceNotes: Correct. A negative bit line assists the write.
Lowering, not raising, the cell supply during a write makes the cell easier to flip.
Lowering the word line weakens the access transistor and makes writing harder.

sram-flash-048.question: In multi-level (MLC or TLC) NAND flash, why are the bit patterns assigned to adjacent threshold-voltage states chosen to differ by only one bit?
choices: So that misreading a state as its neighbor causes only a single-bit error
sram-flash-048.explanation: In multilevel cells, threshold distributions broaden through wear and interference and overlap neighboring states, causing misreads—almost always into an adjacent state. Assigning bit patterns in Gray code, so adjacent states differ by one bit, limits each misread to a single-bit error and minimizes the ECC burden. For TLC's eight states, the order might be 111→110→100→101→001→000→010→011.
choiceNotes: Erasing is still necessary regardless of the assignment.
Correct. A Gray code limits the error to a single bit.
The bit assignment does not double the write speed.

sram-flash-049.question: In 3D NAND, what is the structure called in which the edge of the stack is shaped into steps so that each layer's word line can be connected?
sram-flash-049.explanation: In 3D NAND, hundreds of conductive word-line layers are stacked, so the array edge is etched into a staircase that exposes each layer's top surface for contacts. The steps are formed by repeatedly etching while trimming back the resist, so more layers mean longer processing and more staircase area. Designs split the staircase into multiple rows or add steps in another direction to save area.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is a stepped structure for connecting to each layer.
Damascene is a process of filling trenches with metal to form wiring.
A trench is a groove in the substrate, not a structure for connecting to each layer.

sram-flash-050.question: In 3D NAND, what is the main advantage of placing peripheral circuits such as sense amplifiers beneath the memory array (CMOS under Array and similar)?
choices: It reduces chip area, increasing the capacity obtained from one wafer
It reduces the number of stacked layers
sram-flash-050.explanation: Peripheral circuits traditionally sat beside the cell array; placing them directly beneath it (CMOS under Array, Periphery under Cell, etc.) cuts die area by about 20–30%, raising bit density and lowering cost. Since the periphery is built first, it must withstand the thermal steps of array formation. Approaches that build the periphery and array on separate wafers and bond them (such as CBA) are also in production.
choiceNotes: Erasing is still required regardless of the structure.
Correct. Placing peripherals under the array reduces area.
It is not directly related to the number of layers.
